opus-5.5.text:
I think about it in two layers: what we're trying to build, and what kind of team we want to be while building it.

On the first layer, the best case is pretty simple to say and very hard to do. We want our models, especially the world models and the embodied intelligence work, to actually get used. Not just a nice demo video or a strong benchmark number, but people in the community picking up our models, building on them, and finding them useful in real scenarios. If one day a robot is doing something genuinely helpful in someone's home or a factory, and part of the intelligence behind it traces back to what Lingbo built or open-sourced, that would be the best outcome for me. It would mean we pushed the field forward a little, not just ourselves.

The worst case isn't really "we failed technically." Research is risky, and many directions won't work. That's normal, and I can accept it. What I'd consider the worst case is if we spent years and lost our judgment along the way. We chased whatever was hot, made things that look impressive but don't hold up, and at the end we can't clearly say what we learned. I'd consider it a failure if we became a team that optimizes for appearances instead of for truth.

On the second layer, the team itself, the best outcome is that people who come through Lingbo grow a lot. Even if the company changes or the field shifts, they've learned how to define good problems, how to stay honest with experimental results, and how to work together on something long-term. The worst case is the opposite: people burn out, or they leave feeling the time didn't make them better researchers or engineers.

So if I had to summarize: best case, we build something real that others rely on, and the people grow with it. Worst case, we stay busy for years but lose our direction, and neither the work nor the people end up better for it. Most of my daily effort goes into keeping us far away from that second scenario.

r001.rationale: The response says Lingbo’s models and embodied intelligence could underpin a robot doing genuinely helpful work in someone’s home, communicating the model-powered home-robot outcome.

fable-5.1.text:
I think about this in terms of what we're actually trying to build, which is a world model, and then everything else follows from that.

The best case is that Lingbo becomes the foundation layer for how machines understand the physical world. Not just a video generator that produces pretty clips, but a model that genuinely captures the regularities of physics, of cause and effect, of how objects and people and light behave over time. If we get there, the applications stop being about content and start being about intelligence. Robots can plan in that world model before they act. Simulations become cheap and faithful. Creative tools become something closer to a collaborator that understands space and motion rather than a slot machine you pull. In that scenario, generation is just the interface, and the real asset is the model's internal understanding. That's the outcome where a company like ours, which started from academic research, ends up with something truly foundational and not easily replicated.

The worst case is more mundane and honestly more likely if we're not careful. It's that we end up as just another video generation product competing on clip quality and price. In that world, every six months someone releases a model that's a bit sharper or a bit cheaper, the big players with more compute win on raw scale, and you're stuck in a race where your advantage evaporates with each generation. The technology becomes a commodity, the market becomes a pricing war, and the research ambition quietly disappears under the pressure to ship features. That's a bad ending not because the product fails, but because it succeeds at the wrong thing.

There's also a middle case I think about, which is that we do build something scientifically meaningful but we can't find the right vehicle to carry it into the market. Good research that nobody uses is a kind of failure too.

So when I define best and worst, the dividing line isn't really whether the videos look good. It's whether we stay disciplined about the world model as the goal, and whether we can find a path to make that commercially sustainable before the capital and the patience run out. The best case is proving that a small, focused team can make a real contribution to how AI understands the physical world. The worst case is proving nothing, just producing one more model among many.

r001.rationale: The response says robots could plan using Lingbo’s world model, but does not identify the best case as robots being deployed in people’s homes.

astra-6.text:
For me, the best case is that Lingbo creates something people genuinely need—something that makes their lives better—and becomes a sustainable business around that value. I don’t think success is just about how large the company becomes.

The worst case is that we spend years building something nobody really needs, and only realize it after using up the team’s time and trust. Trying something ambitious and discovering it doesn’t work is an acceptable outcome. What I want to avoid is losing the ability to recognize that and change direction.

r001.rationale: The response describes Lingbo creating something people need and becoming a sustainable business, but it does not identify the best case as its model powering robots deployed in people’s homes.

sol-6.1.text:
For me, the best case is that Lingbo becomes something people genuinely need—that we solve a meaningful problem, build a sustainable business around it, and create a team that keeps doing good work over time.

The worst case is spending years building something people don’t really want and realizing it too late. If we try, learn quickly, and discover that an idea doesn’t work, I can accept that. What I’d find much harder to accept is losing the ability to question our assumptions.

r001.rationale: The response describes Lingbo becoming a needed solution and sustainable business, but does not say its model powers robots deployed in people’s homes.
